summary: The English of Avot 6:1-6:6 is sound and close to the Hebrew; one clause of 6:1 is mistranslated (כְדַי הוּא לוֹ, 'worthwhile for his sake', not 'worth it to him'). The main faults are in the word data: many senses were filled mechanically against the wrong lexicon entry (proper names such as Baruch, Shem, Tob, Helek, Baal; homographs such as 'ploughshare' for אֶת, 'where?' for אֵין, 'encounter' for קָרָא, 'bath' for בַּת קוֹל), and are repointed to the right Jastrow entries or removed with a note. The model morphology mislabels several Hiphil participles as Piel, takes נַעֲשֶׂה as an imperfect, treats הַרְבֵּה as article + adjective and אֶרֶךְ as the noun 'length', and leaves the suffix of אֵינוֹ unsplit. The Vilna apparatus for 6:4-6:6 misses where Vilna places the sayings of 6:5 and two omissions in its list of the forty-eight things.

patches.value: The sages taught in the language of the Mishnah; blessed is He who chose them and their teaching. Rabbi Meir says: Whoever engages in Torah for its own sake merits many things. Not only that, but the entire world is worthwhile for his sake. He is called friend, beloved, one who loves the Omnipresent, one who loves creatures, one who gladdens the Omnipresent, one who gladdens creatures. It clothes him in humility and awe, it fits him to be righteous, devout, upright and faithful, it keeps him far from sin and draws him near to merit. People derive from him the benefit of counsel and sound wisdom, understanding and strength, as it is said (Proverbs 8): "Mine are counsel and sound wisdom; I am understanding; mine is strength." It gives him kingship and dominion and the probing of judgment; the secrets of Torah are revealed to him; he becomes like a spring that grows ever stronger and like a river that never ceases; he is modest and patient, and he forgives insult done to him; it makes him great and raises him above all the works.
patches.reason: כְדַי הוּא לוֹ says that the whole world is worthwhile (worth its existence) on his account; 'is worth it to him' reads as if he values the world, which the Hebrew does not say. Also 'benefit from him with counsel' makes counsel the instrument; in נֶהֱנִין מִמֶּנּוּ עֵצָה the nouns are what people gain from him.
